summary: This informational document describes Khronos, a companion to the NTPv4 client that acts as a watchdog and improves protection against time-shifting attacks. It changes only the client's system process, not the wire protocol. So it can be used with current and future time protocols.

plainLanguage.summary: If someone tries to trick your clock, Khronos asks several clocks and ignores any that look strange, so you can't be fooled about the time.

questions: how many ntp servers does khronos query
subtitle: A security watchdog that protects system clocks from malicious time-shifting attacks.

tldr.problem: Network Time Protocol (NTP) clients synchronize their clocks with remote servers, but attackers can deliberately shift the time on a client's system clock by manipulating NTP servers or intercepting NTP packets, even when encryption and authentication are used. This attack can break cryptography, fraud detection, and other security systems that depend on accurate time.
tldr.mechanism: Khronos is a background security monitor for NTP clients that randomly queries many servers (e.g., 15 out of 500) instead of relying on a few, applies a mathematical algorithm to eliminate suspicious responses, and only updates the clock if the consensus is strong. If the offset becomes too large, Khronos detects an attack and takes over clock control, preventing the shift.
tldr.outcome: An NTP client running Khronos can tolerate an attacker controlling up to one-third of its server pool with negligible risk of successful time-shifting over many years, whereas standard NTPv4 is vulnerable to much weaker attackers.

today: RFC 9523 was published in February 2024 as an Informational document with IETF consensus. It describes Khronos as a companion to NTPv4 that can be deployed on individual clients without requiring changes to servers or the wire protocol. Khronos can be integrated into NTP client implementations or run as a separate background service. The technique represents a major advance in defending against time-shifting attacks for internet-connected systems that use public NTP servers.

sections.title: The NTP time-shifting attack and why it matters
sections.content:
NTP (Network Time Protocol) is the standard way Internet devices synchronize their clocks. A time-shifting attack is when an attacker changes a client's clock by interfering with NTP. This can happen even if NTP is encrypted and authenticated, because an attacker who can delay or drop packets (like through a man-in-the-middle position in the network) or who compromises an NTP server can simply delay the NTP response, causing the client to think the current time is later than it really is. If you shift a computer's clock backwards or forwards, it breaks cryptographic signatures, corrupts financial transactions, invalidates security certificates, and disrupts systems that depend on time sequences.

NTPv4, as originally designed, typically synchronizes with only a handful of servers. This means an attacker who controls just a few servers or who can intercept traffic to those servers has a good chance of shifting the time. RFC 9523 introduces Khronos, a companion security application that dramatically improves NTP's resistance to this attack by being much more suspicious of any individual server.
sections.plainLanguage: If you ask three friends what time it is and one of them lies, they can fool you. But if you ask fifty friends and ignore the three that seem wrong, you get the right time.

sections.title: How Khronos works: sampling, filtering, and consensus
sections.content:
Khronos runs in the background alongside NTPv4, continuously monitoring the client's clock. In each poll interval (roughly every 10 minutes), Khronos randomly selects and queries 10 to 15 servers from a local pool of hundreds of servers. This randomness is crucial for security: an attacker cannot predict which servers will be asked. Khronos collects time offsets from each server and discards outliers—specifically, it removes the lowest third and highest third of the offsets and checks whether the middle third are all close together.

If the remaining offsets pass two safety checks (they are close enough to each other, and their average is close to the client's estimated time from between polls), then Khronos trusts them and uses their average as the official time offset. If the checks fail, Khronos immediately resamples with a different random set of servers and tries again. After several failed attempts, Khronos enters panic mode, querying all servers in its pool and applying the same filtering. This approach spreads queries across the network, preventing attackers from easily predicting or targeting which servers are asked.
sections.plainLanguage: Khronos asks many random clocks, ignores the ones that are way off, and checks if the middle ones agree. If they do not agree, it asks different clocks and tries again.

sections.title: Security guarantees: how much attack does Khronos resist?
sections.content:
Khronos provides strong provable security guarantees. If an attacker controls less than two-thirds of the queried servers, Khronos can always find at least one honest server in the remaining offsets after trimming the extremes. This means the average will be close to the correct time, and Khronos will not be fooled. If an attacker controls more than two-thirds, Khronos has a very low probability of being fooled in a single poll, and the probability of repeated successful attacks decreases exponentially.

For example, with 500 servers in the pool and Khronos querying 15 per interval, if an attacker controls one-seventh of the servers (approximately 71 servers), it would take over 20 years of continuous attack attempts on average to shift the time by just 100 milliseconds. In contrast, standard NTPv4 using only four servers would be compromised almost immediately against such an attacker. The security improvement is enormous: the attacker would need to control far more servers or have many more years. Khronos also resists man-in-the-middle attacks that merely delay packets, whereas NTPv4 can be tricked by such packet-delay attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: If liars are fewer than one-third of the clocks you ask, you will find the truth. Even if there are more liars, you have to ask millions of times before one trick works.

sections.title: Running Khronos in practice
sections.content:
Khronos is designed to work with today's NTP servers without changes to the wire protocol, so it is compatible with all current and future time protocols. When Khronos detects an attack (a large time offset), it notifies the user or system administrator, and the client can take action. Between attack detections, Khronos runs passively; NTPv4 controls the clock and provides normal high-precision timekeeping. This hybrid approach ensures that Khronos does not degrade time accuracy in normal operation.

Khronos requires a local pool of hundreds of NTP servers, gathered by periodic DNS queries to public NTP server pools. The pool should be geographically diverse to make it harder for an attacker to compromise or intercept traffic to a large fraction. Khronos is intended for internet-connected devices and systems that synchronize with public NTP servers. It is not intended for data centers or enterprises that use local atomic clocks, GPS receivers, or private NTP infrastructure, where the threat model is different.
sections.plainLanguage: Khronos sits quietly watching your clock. When things look normal, it lets NTP do its job. When it smells trouble, it takes over and alerts you.
